n: Under the new Persian rule, Darius organizes the empire with 120 regional officials. The Persians were known for this kind of efficient administration.
Three senior administrators oversee the governors to protect the king’s interests, and Daniel is one of them—now an elderly statesman.

f.w: the king should have no damage
f.g: So the king would suffer no loss (from corruption or mismanagement).

n: Daniel stands out because of his “excellent spirit,” and the king plans to put him over the whole kingdom—like Joseph in Egypt.

f.w: an excellent spirit was in him

n: Jealous rivals dig for scandal but find nothing: Daniel is honest, faithful, and careful. His integrity is airtight.

f.w: they could find none occasion nor fault

n: They realize the only way to trap Daniel is through his devotion to God. His faith is his only “weakness” in their eyes.
The conspirators come as a crowd to the king—the Aramaic suggests they came in a throng, perhaps to pressure him.
They falsely claim “all” the officials agree (Daniel obviously didn’t). They propose that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king, under penalty of the lions’ den.

f.g: Ancient Near Eastern kings kept lions in captivity, sometimes for royal hunts.

n: They urge him to make it irrevocable under Persian law, which—once sealed by the king—could not be changed.

f.w: the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not

n: Flattered, Darius signs the decree without seeing the trap.

Daniel knows the law is signed, yet goes home and prays as always—kneeling three times a day by windows open toward Jerusalem, giving thanks. He neither hides nor makes a show; he simply keeps doing what is right.

f.w: his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem

n: The conspirators rush in and catch Daniel praying and pleading with God.
They first get the king to confirm the unchangeable decree before naming their target.
Then they accuse Daniel, sneering at him as an exile from Judah who ignores the king.
The king is furious—with himself. He realizes he has been manipulated and works until sunset trying to find a legal way to save Daniel.
The conspirators return to press the point: Persian law cannot be changed. The king is trapped by his own decree.
Daniel is thrown into the den. The king says, perhaps as a hopeful wish: “Your God, whom you serve continually, will deliver you.”

f.w: Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee

n: A stone seals the den, stamped with the king’s and nobles’ signet rings so no one can tamper with it. Many readers see a parallel to the sealed tomb of Jesus.

f.g: A seal ring pressed into clay or wax as an official signature.

f.w: a stone was brought, and laid upon the mouth of the den

n: The king spends a sleepless night fasting, refusing entertainment—his anxiety shows how much he cares for Daniel.

f.g: The Aramaic word is uncertain—perhaps entertainment or concubines.

n: At first light he hurries to the den.
With anguish he calls out: “Daniel, servant of the living God, was your God able to deliver you?” The phrase “the living God” contrasts with lifeless idols.
Daniel answers with a respectful greeting—he is alive!
God sent His angel to shut the lions’ mouths. Daniel affirms his innocence before God and his loyalty to the king—he was faithful to both.

f.w: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths

n: Daniel is lifted out without a scratch “because he believed in his God.” Faith is named as the key.

f.w: because he believed in his God

n: The accusers and their families are thrown to the lions, which overpower them before they hit the bottom. This harsh punishment reflects Persian practice, not God’s command; it shows the trap turned back on those who set it.

f.w: the lions had the mastery of them

n: Darius issues a proclamation to all nations, much like Nebuchadnezzar’s in chapter 4.
He commands everyone to revere Daniel’s God—the living, eternal God whose kingdom will never be destroyed. Another pagan king testifies of God’s everlasting kingdom.

f.w: his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed

n: God delivers, rescues, and works wonders—as He showed by saving Daniel from the lions.
Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus. Some scholars read this as “Darius, that is, Cyrus the Persian,” suggesting they may be the same person.
